title: Why Do Flamingos Eat Upside Down? (4-5 Pumps a Second) 🦩
description:
Why do flamingos eat with their heads upside down? Their beak is built backwards: a big lower jaw, comb-like plates that sieve water, and a tongue that pumps like a piston to trap shrimp and algae.

topic: Why do flamingos eat with their heads upside down?
script: You've never seen a flamingo eat right-side up. It feeds with its head upside down, because its beak is built backwards. Most birds have a big top beak, and a smaller bottom one. A flamingo's is the other way round. So it flips its head over, and the big lower beak skims the water like a scoop. Inside, the edges are lined with tiny comb-like plates. Then the tongue starts pumping, about four or five times a second, like a little piston. Water squirts out through the combs, and tiny shrimp and algae get trapped inside. Flamingos even stomp in the mud, to stir up little whirlpools full of food. And those shrimp and algae? They're packed with pink pigments. That's what turns a flamingo pink. So, would you eat upside down, if it turned you pink?
key_facts: A flamingo's lower beak is larger and stronger than the upper one, the reverse of most birds (Stanford Birds essay)
Feeding flamingos hold the head upside down with the bill in the water (SDZWA, SeaWorld)
Comb-like lamellae inside the bill filter food (SeaWorld, Stanford)
The tongue pumps water through the bill about 4-5 times a second in Caribbean flamingos (SDZWA 5-6/s, Stanford up to 4/s, SeaWorld 4-5/s)
Flamingos stomp and stir up vortices that draw food in (UC Berkeley, PNAS 2025)
Pink colour comes from carotenoid pigments in algae and invertebrates (SeaWorld)
